newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Kabila defends cabinet, sees elections in 2 years.
newsitem.headline: Kabila defends cabinet, sees elections in 2 years.

text.p: New Congo's self-proclaimed president Laurent Kabila said on Saturday he expected to hold elections after two years and defended his government against charges of autocracy.

He said he believed the cabinet, dominated by his Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo (AFDL), was broad-based, despite criticism of the exclusion of veteran opposition leader Etienne Tshisekedi.
"Democratic election after two years transitional period," Kabila told CNN television during a visit to a Kinshasa hospital, his first public appearance since he arrived in the capital on Tuesday.
"It is a broad-based government," Kabila said of the cabinet, nine of whose 13 ministers are AFDL members.
Troops in Kinshasa fired in the air on Saturday to break up a march by about 1,000 students protesting against Kabila's government.

Some 100 demonstrators were loaded onto trucks and taken to Kinshasa's Camp Kololo military barracks. Information Minister Raphael Ghenda blamed reactionary political forces and said demonstrations were technically banned.

South African Deputy President Thabo Mbeki, who played a key role in attempts to ensure a peaceful transition, said on Friday Congo could not afford to rush into elections and it would be difficult to achieve a fair poll soon after taking power.
Decades of neglect since the end of Belgian colonial rule have left the former Zaire with little working infrastructure, few roads and no state administration to speak of.
The presence of thousands of Rwandan refugees has been cited in the past as an additional complication.
Witnesses said the students taken to the barracks near the city centre were not seen coming out, but Ghenda said they had been taken home.
"In principle, demonstrations have not been permitted in all parts of the country that we have liberated in this period of consolidation, but we are very tolerant," Ghenda told Reuters.
"Today what happened is that reactionary political forces of the former regime manipulated people who claimed to be students."
Mobutu, weakened by cancer, arrived in Morocco on Friday from Togo but an official in Rabat said on Saturday he was expected to go on to France early next month.

With anti-Kabila anger spreading to Tshisekedi's homeland in the centre of the Democratic Republic of Congo, Kabila's admirers in Kinshasa staged a symbolic show of support. Their 150-strong march was allowed to go ahead unhindered.

Residents in Mbuji-Mayi, the diamond mining capital of Tshisekedi's Kasai homeland, said protesters were dispersed by Kabila's soldiers on Friday. Mbuji-Mayi was calm on Saturday with businesses open.
In announcing his incomplete government on Thursday, Kabila not only excluded Tshisekedi but also abolished the post of prime minister -- which the radical politician claims.

Saturday's Potentiel newspaper said the people of the new Congo feared a return to dictatorship. "They see from the first political acts of the new rulers that we are heading towards a single party state," it said.
Borders remained closed on Saturday, but Transport Minister Henri Mova said there was no technical reason for the measure and that regular flights could start by Tuesday.
Mova told a news conference that security considerations were to blame for the fact that travellers had been stopped from leaving Kinshasa.
